title: Dynamic Energy Dispatch Strategy for Integrated Energy System Based on Constrained Reinforcement Learning
abstract_preview: —An integrated energy system includes multiple subsystems of electricity, heating, and gas. It is difficult to achieve dynamic dispatch of multi-energy flows due to challenges in establishing detailed mathematical models and the impacts of uncertain factors. Reinforcement learning has the ability to fit non-convex and non-linear problems. It avoids simplifying detailed mathematical models and complex, uncertain factors in the solution process, like traditional methods, which provides a new idea for achieving dynamic energy dispatch. However, existing research generally relies on soft constraints, such as reward function penalties, to obtain the dispatch strategy, which may violate the system’s operational safety. This paper ensures the security of dynamic energy dispatch strategies by adding two constraint mechanisms on reinforcement learning. First, boundary conditions of the action security domain are established through continuous interaction and feedback between the agent and the environment. It can effectively restrict infeasible actions. Second, the strategy is constrained by the truncation function in the trust domain, and strategy update is always kept within a controllable range to improve convergence and stability of the IES dynamic energy dispatch model. Finally, simulation results indicate that the proposed method can effectively constrain agent action selections and strategy updates during the dynamic energy dispatch process. This is of great significance to ensure the safe and stable operation of the system. Index Terms—Constrained reinforcement learning, dynamic energy dispatch, integrated energy system, security issue. ## I. INTRODUCTION HE conflict between energy demand and environmental T protection is becoming increasingly severe worldwide. Therefore, establishing an integrated energy system (IES) with interconnected heterogeneous energy networks and complementary use of multiple resources is crucial to achieving lowcarbon and sustainable development [1]–[3]. IES includes multiple subsystems of electricity, heating, and gas. Compared with the electric network, the infrastructures of the heating network and the natural gas network are easily prone to aging. At the same time, intermittent energy sources such as wind power and photovoltaics are widely used in the electric network. Therefore, IES’s complexity and uncertainty have become more apparent. How to perform real-time, accurate, and safe, dynamic energy dispatch in this situation has become a new research direction [4], [5]. Now, the problem has been investigated using scenario analysis, robust optimization, and model predictive control. In [6], considering the uncertainty of intermittent energy sources and load in a combined heat and power microgrid, the system optimization dispatch problem based on robust optimization is studied. In [7], a two-layer robust model is constructed using an uncertainty approach to obtain a system dispatch scheme for the worst-case scenario. The above references require establishing accurate mathematical models and are mostly limited to a fixed dispatch plan. It cannot dynamically respond to the impacts of system structure changes, network infrastructures’ aging, and random fluctuations in source and load. Reference [8] proposes a model-based predictive control method for dynamic dispatch of cold-heat-electricity cogeneration type microgrids, which can optimize the device output based on rolling optimization. In [9], a model predictive control method is used to optimize the output of each device for grid-connected building energy systems. Although the above research can effectively deal with uncertain factors and optimize equipment output in real-time, it still relies on fixed system parameter settings and accurate prediction of intermittent energy output. It also cannot be effectively applied to the entire life cycle of system operation. In recent years, under widespread application of artificial intelligence technology, reinforcement learning has provided a new idea for solving the problems mentioned above [10]– [12]. Reinforcement learning is a data-driven method. It has better adaptive learning ability and decision-making ability for non-convex, non-linear problem optimization. Therefore, it avoids simplifying the non-convex and non-linear parts of the model to solve the problem, unlike the traditional method. At the same time, reinforcement learning focuses on how the agent takes actions in the environment to obtain maximum cumulative reward, which is consistent with the dynamic dispatch of the integrated energy system. It focuses on how the system makes decisions to obtain optimal operating cost in a particular dispatch period [13], [14]. At present, reinforcement learning has been preliminarily applied to the economic dispatch problem of the IES. In [15], the Q learning algorithm is combined with game theory to optimize the dispatch problem of the smart grid. In [16], the deep Q learning network was used to solve the real-time dispatch strategy of the microgrid. However, all the above methods require discretization of action and suffer from the obvious challenge of dimensional disaster. In [17], the uncertain economic dispatch of the IES based on the DDPG algorithm can effectively deal with continuous state and action spaces. However, the algorithm is sensitive to parameters, and it is a daunting task to adjust them. In [18], the CPO algorithm is used to study optimal dispatch of microgrids. Policy updates are constrained by Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence but suffer from disadvantages such as excessive computational effort and long training time. Therefore, it is not suitable for practical engineering. Additionally, a common problem with existing research is the over-reliance on reward functions for unconstrained exploration, which can easily lead to dispatch decisions that violate the system’s operational safety [19]. Analyzing the shortcomings of existing methods, it was found that there is still a gap between the front-end of academic research and practical applications based on datadriven methods. As a black-box model, the reinforcement learning method of data-driven theory still needs further study, algorithm convergence, and result security verification. This paper formulates the IES multi-energy flow dynamic dispatch problem within a data-driven framework. It proposes an optimization solution strategy for IES dynamic energy dispatch based on a constrained reinforcement learning algorithm. The specific performance is as follows: 1) The proposed method is based on data-driven theory, which can avoid simplifying non-convex and non-linear parts of the model to solve the problem. It can use interactive data with the environment to dynamically respond to system changes, such as system structure changes, infrastructure aging, and impact of uncertain factors. 2) Aiming at the security issues caused by traditional reinforcement learning relying on the reward function for unconstrained exploration, boundary conditions of the action security domain are used to restrict the selection of actions, which effectively avoids over-limit actions of the IES units. 3) Aiming at the instability of decision-making results caused by the influence of uncertain external factors. In the trust domain, the strategy update is constrained by the truncation function, and the strategy update is always kept within a controllable range to improve the convergence and stability of the IES optimal dispatch decision-making model. ## II. IES DYNAMIC ENERGY DISPATCH MATHEMATICAL MODEL The goal of IES dynamic energy dispatch is to pursue economic optimization under the premise of ensuring safety. Thus, IES effectively arranges the output of various devices in each period under the premise of meeting user load requirements and system operation safety [20]. This paper takes the IES shown in Fig. 1 as an example. It is a complex system composed of an electric network, a heating network, and a natural gas network. The system also includes a variety of devices, such as combined heat and power units (CHP), photovoltaics (PV), battery energy storage (BES), gas boilers (GB), electric boilers (EB), and electricity/heat loads. ![](7e16467e23dbe99887458c3b9d9edd0ec01d5b1118e0495f756304769eae8efd.jpg) Fig. 1. Schematic diagram of the integrated energy system. ## A. Objective Function Since IES dynamic energy dispatch needs to take into account the mutual influence between different dispatch periods, minimizing the expected value of the total cost of all dispatch periods is considered as the objective function [21]. $$ \min E \left(\sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} F (t)\right) = E \left(\sum_ {t = 1} ^ {T} \left(F _ {\mathrm{e}} (t) + F _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t)\right)\right)\tag{1} $$ where $T$ is the length of the dispatch period; $F _ { \mathrm { e } } ( t )$ is the cost of purchasing energy at time step $t ;$ and, $F _ { \mathrm { B E S } } ( t )$ is the charge or discharge depreciation cost of BES at time step t. ## 1) Cost of Purchasing Energy The cost of purchasing energy at time step t can be expressed as: $$ \begin{array}{r l} & F _ {\mathrm{e}} (t) = \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{e}} (t) p _ {\mathrm{grid}} (t) \Delta t \\ & \qquad + \varepsilon_ {\mathrm{gas}} (t) \left(\frac {p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t) \Delta t}{\eta_ {\mathrm {CHP\_P}}} + \frac {h _ {\mathrm{GB}} (t) \Delta t}{\eta_ {\mathrm{GB}}}\right) \end{array}\tag{2} $$ where $p _ { \mathrm { g r i d } } ( t )$ is the exchanged power between the IES and the main grid at time step t. If the value is positive, it means that the system purchases electricity from the main grid, and if it is negative, it means that the surplus power of the system is sold to the grid. p<sub>CHP</sub>(t) is the electric power output of CHP; $h _ { \mathrm { G B } } ( t )$ is the heat output of GB; η<sub>CHP P</sub> is the electrical efficiency of the CHP; η<sub>GB</sub> is the efficiency of ${ \mathrm { G B } } ; \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { e } } ( t )$ and $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { g a s } } ( t )$ are the purchase price of electricity and natural gas at time step t, respectively; and $\Delta t$ is time interval. ## 2) Cost of Battery Storage Depreciation Charge and discharge depreciation cost of BES can be expressed as: $$ F _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t) = \rho_ {\mathrm{BES}} | p _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t) |\tag{3} $$ where $p _ { \mathrm { B E S } } ( t )$ is the charging/discharging power of BES at time step t. The positive and negative values of $p _ { \mathrm { B E S } } ( t )$ respectively, denote discharging and charging. ρ<sub>BES</sub> is depreciation cost factor for BES. ## B. Constraints IES dynamic energy dispatch includes a series of constraints such as power balance, external energy supply, and equipment operation. ## 1) Power Balance Constraints Neglecting the system’s network loss, the balance between generation and load constraints at time step t can be expressed as: $$ p _ {\mathrm{load}} (t) = p _ {\mathrm{grid}} (t) + p _ {\mathrm{PV}} (t) + p _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t) + p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t) - p _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t)\tag{4} $$ $$ h _ {\mathrm{load}} (t) = h _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t) + h _ {\mathrm{GB}} (t) + h _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t)\tag{5} $$ where $p _ { \mathrm { P V } } ( t )$ is the output of $\mathrm { P V } ; p _ { \mathrm { E B } } ( t )$ is the input electrical power of EB; $h _ { \mathrm { E B } } ( t )$ is the heat power output of EB; $h _ { \mathrm { C H P } } ( t )$ is the heat power output of CHP; and, $p _ { \mathrm { l o a d } } ( t )$ and $h _ { \mathrm { l o a d } } ( t )$ are the electrical load and heat load, respectively. ## 2) IES and Main Grid Interactive Power Constraints Considering operational stability on the grid side, there are upper and lower constraints on power interaction between the main grid and the IES. $$ P _ {\mathrm{grid}} ^ {\mathrm{min}} \leq p _ {\mathrm{grid}} (t) \leq P _ {\mathrm{grid}} ^ {\mathrm{max}}\tag{6} $$ where $P _ { \mathrm { g r i d } } ^ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $P _ { \mathrm { g r i d } } ^ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are the upper and lower limits of the interaction power between IES and the main grid, respectively. ## 3) Device Operation Constraints Taking the IES selected in this paper as a case, the upper and lower limits of the electrical power of CHP, charging/ discharging power of BES, the heat power of GB, and the heat power of EB can be expressed as: $$ P _ {\mathrm{CHP}} ^ {\mathrm{min}} \leq p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t) \leq P _ {\mathrm{CHP}} ^ {\mathrm{max}}\tag{7} $$ $$ P _ {\mathrm{BES}} ^ {\mathrm{min}} \leq p _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t) \leq P _ {\mathrm{BES}} ^ {\mathrm{max}}\tag{8} $$ $$ H _ {\mathrm{GB}} ^ {\mathrm{min}} \leq h _ {\mathrm{GB}} (t) \leq H _ {\mathrm{GB}} ^ {\mathrm{max}}\tag{9} $$ $$ H _ {\mathrm{EB}} ^ {\mathrm{min}} \leq h _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t) \leq H _ {\mathrm{EB}} ^ {\mathrm{max}}\tag{10} $$ where $P _ { \mathrm { C H F } } ^ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $P _ { \mathrm { C H P } } ^ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are the upper and lower limits of the electric power of CHP, respectively; $H _ { \mathrm { E B } } ^ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $H _ { \mathrm { E B } } ^ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are the upper and lower limits of the heat power of EB, respectively. ## 4) Device Output Ramp Rate Constraints The output of each device in IES needs to meet upward and downward ramp rate constraints. $$ - R _ {\mathrm{CHP}} ^ {\mathrm{down}} \Delta t \leq p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t) - p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t - 1) \leq R _ {\mathrm{CHP}} ^ {\mathrm{up}} \Delta t\tag{11} $$ $$ - R _ {\mathrm{GB}} ^ {\mathrm{down}} \Delta t \leq h _ {\mathrm{GB}} (t) - h _ {\mathrm{GB}} (t - 1) \leq R _ {\mathrm{GB}} ^ {\mathrm{up}} \Delta t\tag{12} $$ $$ - R _ {\mathrm{EB}} ^ {\mathrm{down}} \Delta t \leq h _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t) - h _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t - 1) \leq R _ {\mathrm{EB}} ^ {\mathrm{up}} \Delta t\tag{13} $$ where $R _ { \mathrm { C H P } } ^ { \mathrm { u p } } , R _ { \mathrm { C H P } } ^ { \mathrm { d o w n } } , R _ { \mathrm { G B } } ^ { \mathrm { u p } } , R _ { \mathrm { G B } } ^ { \mathrm { d o w n } } , R _ { \mathrm { E B } } ^ { \mathrm { u p } }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { E B } } ^ { \mathrm { d o w n } }$ are the upward and downward ramping rates of CHP, GB and EB, respectively. ## 5) BES Constraints BES should consider the impact of excessive charging/ discharging during its operation. As a result, state of charge (SOC) of BES needs to be limited within a certain range. $$ C _ {\mathrm{SOC}} ^ {\mathrm{min}} \leq c _ {\mathrm{SOC}} (t) \leq C _ {\mathrm{SOC}} ^ {\mathrm{max}}\tag{14} $$ where $C _ { \mathrm { S O C } } ^ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $C _ { \mathrm { S O C } } ^ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ are the upper and lower limits of the BES state of charge, respectively; $c _ { \mathrm { S O C } } ( t )$ is the state of charge of BES at time step $t . c _ { \mathrm { S O C } } ( t )$ can be determined using the following equation as: $$ c _ {\mathrm{SOC}} (t) = c _ {\mathrm{SOC}} (t - 1) - \frac {\eta_ {\mathrm{BES}} p _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t) \Delta t}{Q _ {\mathrm{BES}}}\tag{15} $$ $$ c _ {\mathrm{SOC}} (0) = C _ {\mathrm{SOC}} ^ {\mathrm{ini}}\tag{16} $$ where $Q _ { \mathrm { B E S } }$ is BES capacity; $C _ { \mathrm { S O C } } ^ { \mathrm { i n i } }$ is the initial state of charge of BES; η<sub>BES</sub> is the charging/discharging coefficient for BES, which can be expressed as: $$ \eta_ {\mathrm{BES}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \eta_ {\mathrm{ch}} & p _ {\mathrm{BES}} < 0 \\ \frac {1}{\eta_ {\mathrm{dis}}} & p _ {\mathrm{BES}} \geq 0 \end{array} \right.\tag{17} $$ where $\eta _ { \mathrm { c h } }$ and $\eta _ { \mathrm { d i s } }$ are the charging and discharging efficiency of BES, respectively. 6) Coupling Link of Electric Network and Heating Network This paper considers two coupling devices, including EB and CHP. EB can be regarded as the electric network’s load and the heating network’s source, consuming electricity to generate heat. CHP can be regarded as the load of the natural gas network, the source of the electric network, and the heating network. It mainly generates electricity by consuming natural gas, and waste heat can also provide heat energy for users. For EB, $$ p _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t) = \frac {h _ {\mathrm{EB}} (t)}{\eta_ {\mathrm{EB}}}\tag{18} $$ where η<sub>EB</sub> is the conversion efficiency of electricity to heat. For CHP, the coupling relationship between its output of electric power and heat power is called an electric-heat characteristic. CHP in this paper uses the method of determining the heat-to-electricity ratio. $$ p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t) = \frac {h _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t)}{\eta_ {\mathrm{CHP}}}\tag{19} $$ where $\eta _ { \mathrm { C H P } }$ is heat-to-electricity ratio of CHP. ## 7) Uncertainty Distribution of Power and Load Output Due to privacy protection and copyright issues, we are not allowed to use actual confidential data in this paper. Therefore, we generalized the data, mainly load data, by combining actual data and simulated data to form experimental data in this work, in which simulated data is obtained by simulations with a distribution function. Experimental data still hold the general characteristics of load in an integrated energy system and qualify for verification of the proposed method [22]. This function can be expressed as: $$ f (P _ {\mathrm{sto}}) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi} \sigma} \exp \left[ - \frac {(P _ {\mathrm{sto}} - \mu) ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}} \right]\tag{20} $$ where $P _ { \mathrm { s t o } }$ is uniformly expressed as electrical load, heat load, and photovoltaic output; $\mu$ and σ are the expected and standard deviation of the distribution, respectively. At the same time, considering that the constrained reinforcement learning method proposed in this paper is not limited to a single distribution function, in order to further verify its applicability to photovoltaic and load fluctuations, the following two measures are added based on the above simulation data: 1) randomness of the distribution interval is superimposed based on historical data and simulated data 2) random sampling is performed within the constraint interval of the initial state. Together, they form the training data for the reinforcement learning model. ## III. CONSTRAINED REINFORCEMENT LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR IES DYNAMIC DISPATCH PROBLEM The IES dynamic energy dispatch mathematical model in Section II was transformed into a constrained reinforcement learning framework following a Markovian Decision Process [23]. This part is mainly used to explain critical parameter settings of the reinforcement learning method, which is to transform the specific physical problem studied in this paper into a detailed reinforcement learning practical application process. ## A. Constrained Environment Model The constrained environment model refers to the IES that interacts with the agent. Every control action given by the agent through reinforcement learning can obtain corresponding feedback rewards in this constrained environment. The environmental model in this paper mainly includes the power system, natural gas system, and related constrained links, which are expressed by (1) through (20). ## B. State Space The state space is a concrete representation of the environment in which the agent is currently located. States of the IES dynamic dispatch include $p _ { \mathrm { l o a d } } ( t ) , h _ { \mathrm { l o a d } } ( t ) , p _ { \mathrm { P V } } ( t )$ , and $c _ { \mathrm { s o c } } ( t - 1 )$ ). Therefore, the state space can be defined as: $$ s _ {t} = [ p _ {\mathrm{load}} (t), h _ {\mathrm{load}} (t), p _ {\mathrm{PV}} (t), c _ {\mathrm{soc}} (t - 1) ]\tag{21} $$ ## C. Action Space The action space consists of decisions made by the agent through reinforcement learning, and the output of each device can represent an action. h<sub>CHP</sub>(t), h<sub>EB</sub>(t), p<sub>EB</sub>(t) and $p _ { \mathrm { g r i d } } ( t )$ can be derived from p<sub>CHP</sub>(t), p<sub>BES</sub>(t) and $h _ { \mathrm { G B } } ( t ) ~ [ 2 4 ] .$ , so to simplify analysis, action variables are reduced to 3. Action space can be expressed as: $$ a _ {t} = [ p _ {\mathrm{CHP}} (t), p _ {\mathrm{BES}} (t), h _ {\mathrm{GB}} (t) ]\tag{22} $$ ## D. State Transition Probability State transition probability is the agent will move from current state $s _ { t }$ to new state $s _ { t + 1 }$ after performing the selected action $a _ { t }$ . For the IES dynamic dispatch problem, $c _ { \mathrm { s o c } } ( t )$ in the state at the next moment after the agent makes an action can be obtained from (15). The remaining uncertainty state values $p _ { \mathrm { l o a d } } ( t ) , ~ h _ { \mathrm { l o a d } } ( t )$ , and $p _ { \mathrm { P V } } ( t )$ can only be obtained after the agent has interacted with the environment. Together, these variables make up the state transition probability. ## E. Reward Function and Discount Factor First, for the IES dynamic dispatch problem, the agent reward function designed in this paper consists of system operating costs, BES depreciation costs, and action violation constraint penalties. Second, minimization of the IES dispatch cost is transformed into maximization of the reward function. Meanwhile, to prevent the model from converging to a failure, the value needs to be scaled if the reward function is too large. Therefore, the reward function obtained by the agent at time step t can be expressed as: $$ \begin{array}{c} r _ {t} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) = - \frac {1}{1 0 0 0} (F _ {\mathrm{e}} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) + F _ {\mathrm{BES}} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) \\ + F _ {\mathrm{pen}} (s _ {t}, a _ {t})) \end{array}\tag{23} $$ $$ \begin{array}{l} F _ {\mathrm{pen}} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) = \sum_ {i} ^ {N} \max (\max (0, a _ {t} ^ {i} - a ^ {i, \max}), a ^ {i, \min} - a _ {t} ^ {i}) \\ \qquad + \max (\max (0, S _ {\mathrm{oc}, t} - S _ {\mathrm{oc}} ^ {\max}), \\ \qquad S _ {\mathrm{oc}} ^ {\min} - S _ {\mathrm{oc}, t}) + \operatorname{abs} (p _ {t} ^ {\text {supply}} / p _ {t} ^ {\text {load}} - 1) \\ \qquad + \operatorname{abs} (h _ {t} ^ {\text {supply}} / h _ {t} ^ {\text {load}} - 1) \end{array}\tag{24} $$ where $F _ { \mathrm { p e n } } ( s _ { t } , a _ { t } )$ is the penalty for violating constraints; $a _ { t } ^ { i }$ is the action of the i-th unit at time step $t ; p _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { s u p p l y } }$ is the sum of the electric output provided all units at time step $t ; h _ { t } ^ { \mathrm { s u p p l y } }$ is the sum of heat output provided by all units at time step t. IES dynamic dispatch aims to find a policy $\pi ^ { * }$ that maximizes cumulative discount benefit over the whole cycle. $$ J (\pi) = \mathbb {E} _ {\tau \sim \pi} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {T} \gamma^ {t} r _ {t} \right]\tag{25} $$ $$ \pi^ {*} = \operatorname * {a r g m a x} _ {\pi \in \prod_ {\pi}} J (\pi)\tag{26} $$ where $\prod _ { \pi }$ represents the set of policy π; discount factor $\gamma$ indicates the importance of the reward at the future moment to the current reward. For dynamic energy dispatch, decisions made in the current dispatch period have an essential impact on subsequent ones, so it should be taken as a more significant value. In this paper, this value of $\gamma$ is set 0.8. ## IV. CONSTRAINED REINFORCEMENT LEARNING ALGORITHM FOR SOLVING IES DYNAMIC DISPATCH PROBLEM Traditional reinforcement learning algorithms generally obtain optimal strategies by maximizing rewards. This process is unconstrained exploration. However, in practical applications, some explorations will hurt the safe and stable operation of the system, which is not allowed [25], [26]. Therefore, this paper adds constraint measures based on traditional methods and then proposes the Constrained Proximal Policy Optimization (CPPO) algorithm to solve this problem. First, the CPPO algorithm is based on the AC framework. AC framework combines policy learning and value learning to make the model easier to converge. It approximates policy π<sub>θ</sub> through the actor neural network, estimates advantage function $A _ { \pi _ { - } \theta }$ through the critic neural network, and then evaluates and improves current policy $\pi _ { \theta }$ [27]. Second, security domain boundary conditions are added to enforce constraints in the action selection process. Third, the importance sampling technique is used in the policy update process to convert the policy update method from on-policy to off-policy. Ratio of old and new policies is truncated in the trust domain. These compulsory restraints always keep strategy updates within a controllable range, effectively alleviating the impact of uncertain factors on the security of dispatch strategies [28]. ## A. Action Security Domain Boundary In order to ensure the decision results of the reinforcement learning model meet security requirements, boundary conditions of the security domain are added to restrict action. Boundary conditions of the security domain can be gradually improved as the model is trained offline and judgments are made before actual action is executed. If the selected action in the current state is not in the security domain, the action will be forced to skip and wait for a new round of action decision results. ## 1) Action Constraint If action $a _ { t + 1 }$ selected by the agent from state $s _ { t }$ to state $s _ { t + 1 }$ causes a security issue, the action will be restricted, and the action will be stored in constraint set $C _ { s \_ t }$ of state $s _ { t }$ ## 2) Action Permissibility If action $a _ { t + 1 }$ selected by the agent from state $s _ { t }$ to state $s _ { t + 1 }$ is not in constraint set $C _ { s \_ t }$ of state $s _ { t } ,$ , it is considered to be allowed to be executed. ## 3) Skip Action Suppose the action obtained from the model decision is outside the security domain boundary in an actual-world application. In that case, the action is forced to skip and wait for the outcome of the next decision. When the agent selects action $a _ { t } ^ { i } , ~ a _ { t } ^ { i } \in a _ { t }$ of the i-th unit under state $s _ { t } .$ , it appears that the sum of the power provided by the units exceed the load demand. Then the constraint interval of the corresponding action in state $s _ { t }$ is $X _ { s \_ t } = [ a ^ { i , \operatorname* { m i n } } , a _ { t } ^ { i } ]$ As training proceeds, the action constraint interval is updated to $X _ { s \_ t } = [ a ^ { i , \operatorname* { m i n } } , a _ { t } ^ { i \prime } ]$ if action $a _ { t } ^ { i \prime }$ still occurs in state $s _ { t }$ with the unit providing more power than the load demand and $a _ { t } ^ { i \prime } < a _ { t } ^ { i }$ . Similarly, when the power provided by units is less than the load demand, the constraint action interval is set to $X _ { s _ { - } t } = [ a _ { t } ^ { i } , a ^ { i , \operatorname* { m a x } } ]$ . Then action constraint set $X _ { s \_ t } ,$ state $s _ { t } ,$ state $s _ { t + 1 } ,$ , action $a _ { t } .$ , and reward function r are combined to form a set $( s _ { t } , a _ { t } , r _ { t } , s _ { t + 1 } , X _ { s _ { - } t } )$ and stored in the experience replay buffer. Through repeated training in a simulated environment, the model can gradually refine action constraint set $X _ { s _ { - } }$ <sub>t</sub> corresponding to state $s _ { t } .$ Thus, we can set $X _ { s \_ t }$ <sub>t</sub> as the boundary of the action security domain. In the actual environment, it is judged whether the selected action meets the requirements of the security domain boundary. If it is not satisfied, the action will be forced to empty and wait for a new round of action decisions; if it is satisfied, each unit will execute the corresponding actions according to the decision result. ## B. Constraint Update of Policy In the traditional reinforcement learning parameter update process, the gradient itself only provides local first-order information under current parameter θ and ignores the curvature of the surface of the reward function defined according to the actual problem. If a larger step size is selected in a highly curved area, then the algorithm is prone to a sudden drop in performance; on the contrary, if the step size is too small, it can fail to converge for a long time. Even more, the gradient needs to be estimated from samples collected based on the current policy $\pi _ { \theta }$ . Fluctuations in policy performance can, in turn, affect the quality of the collected samples, which further increases the degree of fluctuation during policy updates and raises the issue of system operational safety [29]. The purpose of introducing Theorems 1 and 2 in this paper is to illustrate how to transform the optimal scheduling problem of an integrated energy system into a constrained reinforcement learning process [30]. Actor Neural Network Based on the above theorem, the importance sampling technique is adopted. Two actor networks with the same structure and different parameters are used to complete the approximate policy task jointly [31]. The sampling actor network interacts with the environment to obtain sampled data continuously, and the sampled data is reused to train the updated policy actor network. ## 1) Sampling Actor Network Given that traditional reinforcement learning uses an onpolicy approach, actor network parameters will change after training with sampled data once. As a result, original data can no longer be used, and new data must be collected by interacting with the environment again. This results in much interaction with the environment during training, which reduces training efficiency and lengthens training time. The CPPO algorithm uses important sampling techniques to convert the on-policy method to an off-policy method during policy updates, allowing the training of an actor network based on parameter $\theta$ using data sampled from an actor network on parameter $\theta ^ { \prime } .$ . Parameter $\theta ^ { \prime }$ is fixed in this process. Data from parameter network can be reused to train parameter θ network several times, increasing data utilization and improving training speed. The sampling actor network has the same structure as the policy actor network. According to the following equation, the sampling actor network parameters are updated at regular intervals. $$ \theta^ {\prime} \leftarrow \alpha \theta + (1 - \alpha) \theta^ {\prime}\tag{31} $$ where α is a weighting factor. ## 2) Policy Actor Network Given the constrained policy update equation (30) has a KL divergence constraint term, the gradient descent algorithm is difficult to solve directly. Therefore, it is considered from two aspects: ensuring the stability of policy updates and simplifying calculations. First, the KL divergence constraint is replaced by the truncation function method, and the objective function is truncated. Subsequently, the smaller of the truncated and non-truncated objective functions is taken to reduce the fluctuation of the policy, so the direction of the policy update shows stable improvement. Stochastic quantities of intermittent energy output and load demand are superimposed on historical operating data of the system, which is used as input data for the establishment of the simulation environment and training of the agent model. In the simulated environment, the agent adapts itself to intermittent energy and load uncertainty changes using continuous interaction with the environment while gradually refining the action security domain boundary. In an actual environment, optimal dispatch actions for the units are obtained by passing real-time data into the agent model. If the action does not meet the requirements of the action security domain, the action is forced to skip, and the result of the next round of agent decisions is awaited. Each unit will execute the corresponding action according to the decision result if the action meets the requirements. In the meantime, experience learned in the actual environment can be updated regularly to improve the agent’s real-time decisionmaking ability. Agent’s optimal solution process based on the CPPO algorithm is as follows: 1) State $s _ { t }$ is fed into the policy actor network to obtain mean $\mu _ { \theta }$ and logarithmic variance $\log ( \sigma _ { \theta } ^ { 2 } )$ . The variance is obtained indirectly by the $\sigma _ { \theta } ^ { 2 } ( s ) = \exp ( \rho )$ formula. Then, they are used to construct a normal distribution function representing action distribution. CONCLUSION Aiming at the problem of IES dynamic energy dispatch, this paper proposes an IES dynamic energy dispatch strategy based on a constrained reinforcement learning algorithm. The conclusions are as follows: 1) The proposed method is based on data-driven theory. It can use interactive data to modify the model and dynamically respond to system changes. 2) The proposed method adds constraints based on traditional reinforcement learning.
